concept.name: Recency bias
concept.definition: A cognitive bias that assigns disproportionate weight to recent events over older ones when forming judgments or forecasts, related to the recency effect in memory research. In markets it manifests as extrapolating the latest trend, returns, or volatility into the future at the expense of long-run base rates.
concept.intuition: After three green months it feels like the market only goes up; after a crash it feels like it will never recover.
concept.mechanics: Recent observations are more available in memory and receive excessive weight, so expectations, allocations, and risk perception track the recent past rather than the full sample; investor-behavior commentary documents its role in chasing recent performance and abandoning assets after recent declines.
concept.failure_modes: As an implicit forecasting rule it fails worst at regime changes, which cluster exactly where recency-weighted expectations are most extreme. It should not be confused with the distinct primacy effect, nor with rational updating when trends are genuinely persistent.
concept.misconceptions: Weighting recent data more heavily is not always irrational - in non-stationary markets some recency weighting is optimal; the bias is overweighting beyond what the evidence supports. It is also not the same as price momentum, an empirical return pattern rather than a judgment error.
concept.example: An investor who held a stock through a long rally assumes the uptrend will continue and adds near the top, then refuses to buy during a recession because recent price action feels predictive.
